name: High seas (beyond 200 nautical miles)
who_owns: No country owns it. The sea is open to every country, and each ship answers to the country whose flag it flies. Nothing in the treaty gives a private person a right of their own: the freedoms are written as freedoms of States.

rules.says: Defines the high seas as all sea outside the EEZ, territorial sea, internal waters and archipelagic waters of any State.

The high seas are open to all States. Freedoms listed include navigation, overflight, laying cables and building artificial islands, the last one 'subject to Part VI' (continental shelf rules) and 'permitted under international law'.
No State may validly claim any part of the high seas as its own.
A ship sails under one flag only and answers to that flag State on the high seas.
A warship may board a foreign ship if it reasonably suspects piracy, slave trade, unauthorized broadcasting, a false flag, or that the ship has no nationality.
Since 17 January 2026, the treaty covers areas beyond national jurisdiction. Parties must assess the environmental impact of planned activities under their control there before authorizing them.

hook: Lack of a flag. A structure or vessel with no flag State can be boarded under Art. 110(1)(d). Its people also remain nationals of their home countries, and a country such as the US claims criminal jurisdiction over 'any place outside the jurisdiction of any nation' for offenses by or against its nationals (18 USC 7(7)).
can_you_build: Physically: tow or sail a vessel or platform out, and resupply it from a port, which puts you under that port's law each visit. Legally: register it with a willing flag State, which means accepting that State's law on board. Beyond 200 nm the seabed may still be another country's extended continental shelf (Art. 76) or the ISA-run Area, so anchoring raises separate questions.
facts: Approximately 58.6% of the sea surface is high seas, by MarineRegions' calculation.
Parliamentarians for Global Action puts the high seas at 43% of Earth's surface. Another advocacy page on the same site says 'about half'; the figures depend on the definition used.
The ocean covers more than 70% of Earth's surface (NOAA).
UNCLOS: 172 parties, in force since 16 November 1994. The United States is outside it, per the A&O Shearman briefing on seabed rules.
BBNJ Agreement: adopted 19 June 2023, in force 17 January 2026, 145 signatories and 105 parties on the UN status page read in November 2026. First Conference of the Parties: 11 to 22 January 2027.
BBNJ adds rules on marine genetic resources (no State may claim sovereignty over them, Art. 11), marine protected areas, environmental impact assessment and capacity-building.

name: Exclusive economic zone and continental shelf (12 to 200 nm, sometimes further)
who_owns: The nearest coastal country. It does not own the water outright, but it holds the rights to resources and the exclusive right to authorize artificial islands and structures there. Other countries keep freedom of navigation and overflight.

rules.says: The coastal State has sovereign rights over resources in a zone up to 200 nm from its baselines.
The coastal State has the exclusive right to build and to authorize artificial islands, and installations with economic purposes or that could interfere with its rights.
It has exclusive jurisdiction over such structures, including customs, tax, health, safety and immigration law.
Artificial islands are not islands. They have no territorial sea of their own and do not change any maritime boundary.
Safety zones around structures may reach 500 metres at most, unless international standards allow more.
Shelf rights over seabed resources do not depend on occupation, and Art. 60 applies equally to structures on the shelf.
Other States keep navigation, overflight and cable freedoms in the EEZ, with due regard for the coastal State.
The coastal State may board and arrest to enforce its fishing rules, and may chase a ship out to sea in hot pursuit for violations in the zone.

hook: Art. 60: any platform in the EEZ needs the coastal State's permission, and its tax and immigration laws apply there. In 2019 Thailand's navy raided a floating home anchored just over 12 nm off Phuket and said the occupants had endangered national sovereignty, an offense punishable by life imprisonment or death.
can_you_build: You can sail through freely. To stay on a fixed structure, you need the coastal State's authorization, which puts you under its law by treaty. That rules out a sovereign project here unless the coastal State agrees to carve out a zone (see host-state-carve-outs).
facts: Total area of 230 EEZs: 136,850,878 km², excluding joint regimes and overlapping claims (Flanders Marine Institute poster, 2019 data).
Largest EEZ on that poster: Russia at 7,734,809 km², then Australia at 6,871,622 km².
US EEZ: more than 3.4 million square nautical miles (NOAA).

name: Territorial sea (0 to 12 nm)
who_owns: The coastal country has full sovereignty over the water, the seabed under it and the air above it, the same as its land, subject only to foreign ships' right of innocent passage.

rules.says: Coastal State sovereignty extends to the territorial sea, its seabed and the air above it.
A State may set a territorial sea up to 12 nm from its baselines.
The normal baseline is the low-water line on the State's official charts.
Offshore installations and artificial islands do not count as harbour works and do not push the boundary out.
Foreign ships may pass through if the passage does not harm peace, order or security. Staying put to set up a settlement is outside what passage covers (our reading of Art. 18-19).
Submarines must surface and show their flag here.
In a further belt to 24 nm, the State may act to prevent and punish customs, tax, immigration and health offenses.

hook: Ordinary domestic law: you are inside the country. A State can also move the line. The UK extended its territorial waters to 12 nm in 1987, which put Sealand, about 11 to 13 km offshore, in waters recognized as British.
can_you_build: Only with the coastal State's permission and under its law. Any structure here is a domestic building project.
facts: 12 nm is about 22 km.
Sealand sits about 6 to 7 nm off the English coast (Wikipedia).

sources.t: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, full text

name: Reefs, rocks and low-tide elevations
who_owns: Depends on where it sits and whether it stays dry at high tide. A feature covered at high tide cannot be claimed by occupation, according to the 2016 South China Sea tribunal. It belongs to whichever legal zone it lies in.

rules.says: An island is naturally formed land, surrounded by water, above water at high tide.
Rocks that cannot sustain human habitation or economic life of their own get no EEZ or continental shelf. They still get a 12 nm territorial sea.
A low-tide elevation is natural land above water only at low tide. Beyond 12 nm from land, it has no territorial sea of its own.
Filling in a reef makes an artificial island, which generates no territorial sea.

Mischief Reef, Second Thomas Shoal and Subi Reef are low-tide elevations and are 'not features that are capable of appropriation by occupation or otherwise'. A feature's status depends on its natural condition, before any building.

hook: The tribunal's test looks at the feature's natural state, so dredging sand cannot create a claim. The nearest State also has a practical remedy. Tonga claimed the Minerva Reefs on 24 February 1972, about five weeks after Minerva's declaration, backed by Australia, New Zealand, Fiji, Nauru and Samoa, and sent an expedition that arrived on 18 June 1972.
can_you_build: Building is physically possible on a shallow reef, as Minerva's founders showed by barging in sand from Australia in 1971. Legally it gains you nothing beyond a 500 m safety zone in the best case, and if the reef is inside an EEZ, the coastal State must authorize it under Art. 60.
facts: Minerva: declaration 19 January 1972; in 1982 a group trying to reoccupy was forced off by Tongan troops after three weeks (Wikipedia).
Tribunal finding: no feature in the Spratlys can generate an EEZ, and they cannot do so collectively as a unit.

sources.t: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, full text

name: Abandoned oil platforms and sea forts
who_owns: The law of the location applies, plus the rights of whoever owns the structure. An abandoned platform in an EEZ remains under the coastal State's exclusive jurisdiction, and the treaty requires disused structures to be removed.

rules.says: Abandoned or disused installations must be removed to ensure safe navigation, with any remains publicized.
Coastal State jurisdiction covers installations in the EEZ and on the continental shelf.
A platform has no territorial sea, so it cannot be the base of a claim to surrounding water.
Offshore installations are not part of the coast for drawing boundaries.
Treats all dumping at sea as prohibited unless explicitly permitted.

hook: Art. 60 jurisdiction, plus property and trespass law where the owner is a company or government. Sealand's fort stood outside British waters until the UK extended them in 1987. Rose Island, a purpose-built platform off Rimini, was taken by Italian officers 55 days after declaring independence, then bombed by the Italian Navy in 1969.
can_you_build: Boarding is physically possible and legally weak. Oil platforms stand on a continental shelf, so they normally fall under Art. 60 and 80 of the coastal State. Buying a structure from its owner would transfer ownership only, because jurisdiction under Art. 60 belongs to the State (our reading).
facts: Rose Island: declared 1 May 1968; Italian officers assumed control 26 June 1968; bombed by the navy twice, the second time on 13 February 1969.
Roughs Tower was built by Britain in 1943 and sunk in place on a sandbar (Wikipedia).

sources.t: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, full text

name: Ships under a flag
who_owns: The flag State. On the high seas a ship is under that State's exclusive jurisdiction, and each State sets its own conditions for granting its flag.

rules.says: Every State, including landlocked ones, may sail ships under its flag.
Each State sets the conditions for its flag. There must be a 'genuine link' between State and ship.
One flag only, and exclusive flag-State jurisdiction on the high seas.
A ship using two or more flags as convenient may be treated as having no nationality.
The flag State must keep a register and enforce rules on seaworthiness, crew and safety.
After a collision, only the flag State or the person's own State may bring penal charges.
Each flag State must require masters to rescue people in danger at sea.
Any slave who reaches any ship, under any flag, is free by that fact.
Boarding rights: see high-seas. Art. 110(1)(d) is the one that matters for self-declared flags.

hook: A flag issued by a place no other country recognizes gives no protection. The ship can be treated as having no nationality and boarded. US law, for one, calls a vessel 'without nationality' in several situations and applies its drug law to such vessels (46 USC 70502). With a real flag, the hook is the flag State itself, which keeps jurisdiction over everyone aboard.
can_you_build: This is the easy route: buy a ship and register it in a country that offers a registry. You then live under that country's law on board, and you can be deregistered. A sovereign ship in the legal sense requires a State to back it, which brings you back to recognition.
facts: Flag-State immunity from boarding applies in full only to warships and government non-commercial ships (Art. 95-96).

sources.t: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, full text
46 U.S. Code 70502: Maritime Drug Law Enforcement Act definitions

name: Deep seabed, 'the Area' (run by the ISA)
who_owns: Nobody can own it. The seabed beyond national shelves and its minerals are the common heritage of mankind, and the International Seabed Authority (ISA) in Jamaica controls mineral activities on behalf of all. The water above it remains high seas.

rules.says: The Area and its resources are the common heritage of mankind.
No State or person may claim sovereignty over or appropriate any part of it, and no such claim will be recognized.
Rights in the resources belong to mankind as a whole. Minerals can be sold only under ISA rules.
This regime leaves the status of the water and air above unchanged.
The Area is open to use for peaceful purposes only.
Installations in the Area must be placed and removed under ISA rules, and they cannot have a territorial sea (the text says they 'do not possess the status of islands').
Archaeological and historical objects found there are to be kept for the benefit of mankind.
Operators need sponsorship from a State Party and an approved plan of work.
ISA is the body through which States Parties control activities in the Area; all UNCLOS parties are members.

hook: Art. 137 voids any claim outright. An operator also needs a sponsoring State (Art. 153), so a self-declared country cannot sponsor itself. A rival US route exists: the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act of 1980, under which NOAA found The Metals Company's US subsidiary's application in 'substantial compliance' on 9 March 2026. The ISA's commission is investigating whether that breaches contractors' duties.
can_you_build: You can visit by submersible. Anything mining-related needs a sponsoring State and an ISA contract. Exploitation (commercial mining) rules were still unfinished after the July 2026 Council session, which asked the Secretariat for a roadmap and a new negotiating text.
facts: ISA covers about 54% of the total area of the world's oceans, by its own figure.
ISA members: 172 as of 6 February 2026 (171 States plus the EU).

ISA lists 15-year exploration contracts with 22 contractors. Its text counts 19 nodule contracts, 7 sulphide contracts and 5 crust contracts, which is 31 in all; its sulphide sub-count adds to 8, so the page is not fully consistent.

Exploration only: the March 2026 Council approved no exploitation, and the Mining Code remained unfinished. The July 2026 draft decision says commercial exploitation should not take place without rules.
The US is not party to the UNCLOS deep-sea mining regime (A&O Shearman).

name: Undersea habitats and the water column
who_owns: It follows the surface zone above it. Under the high seas, the water column is high seas and the bottom is either a coastal State's shelf or the ISA's Area. Being underwater does not create a separate legal space.

rules.says: High-seas freedoms apply to the water, so a submerged vessel under a flag is treated as a ship.
In the territorial sea, submarines must travel on the surface with a flag.
Anything fixed to a coastal State's shelf falls under that State.
Anything fixed to the seabed in the Area meets ISA rules and the ban on appropriation.
Research installations follow the rules of the zone where they sit, have no island status, and get 500 m safety zones at most.

hook: Same as the surface zone. The flagless-vessel rule in Art. 110 still applies to a submarine, though a warship has to find it first. Any seabed anchor gives a State or the ISA a physical point of contact.
can_you_build: Moving habitats count as vessels and need a flag. Fixed habitats need a coastal State's authorization or must meet the Area rules. Whether a stationary habitat with a tether on the seabed counts as a ship or an installation has no clear treaty answer (our reading: open).
facts: The seafloor reaches more than 8 km deep in the Mariana Trench (ISA).
Safety zones around research installations: 500 m at most (Art. 260).

sources.t: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, full text

name: Disputed islands (Spratlys, Paracels)
who_owns: Contested by several countries at once, with garrisons on the ground. A newcomer would be a further claimant facing armed occupiers. The 2016 tribunal ruled on maritime zones and said it does not rule on any question of sovereignty over land territory.

rules.says: Rocks get no EEZ or shelf.
No Spratly feature can generate an EEZ, individually or as a group. The tribunal found no legal basis for China to claim historic rights to resources inside the nine-dash line.
China's reclamation at seven features caused severe coral harm and violated its duties, and it built on Mischief Reef inside the Philippine EEZ.
Reclamation creates no new territorial sea.

hook: Armed force on site, and the coastal States' navies. The hook is whichever of them holds the nearest feature. The rule that feature status depends on natural condition means engineering gains you no legal ground.
can_you_build: Practically out of reach, since the islands are garrisoned by rival claimants (see Wikipedia's occupation table). Tomás Cloma's 1956 'Free Territory of Freedomland' claim is catalogued separately.
facts: Natural island area of the Spratlys: 177 ha; about 200 ha counted with reclaimed land in the table used by Wikipedia.
Paracels: over 30 islands, under Chinese control in practice since 1974 (Wikipedia).
The award was issued 12 July 2016 by a tribunal under UNCLOS Annex VII. It is final and binding under Art. 296. China took no part in the proceedings.

sources.t: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, full text

name: Unclaimed land (Bir Tawil, Gornja Siga)
who_owns: Bir Tawil: neither Egypt nor Sudan claims it, because each prefers a different border that gives it the more valuable Halaib Triangle. Gornja Siga: Croatia and Serbia dispute where the border lies, and Croatia controls access on the ground.

rules.says: 'Terra nullius' means territory belonging to no one and open to acquisition by occupation. It is a term of art for how States acquire land.
Land lived on by tribes or peoples with social and political organization was not terra nullius, even if they were nomadic.
A State needs a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and capacity to enter relations with other States.
A State's political existence does not depend on recognition by others.
General international law contains no prohibition on declaring independence. This is a narrow point: the Court did not say a declaration creates a State.

hook: Occupation in the classic sense is an act of a State, so an individual's flag does not do the job (our reading of para 79). The neighbors' border law then becomes the hook. Croatian police have detained and fined entrants at Gornja Siga, sentenced one to 15 days' prison, and removed makeshift buildings in September 2023. Bir Tawil can be reached only through Egypt or Sudan. People also use Bir Tawil, per a paper cited by Wikipedia on the Ababda.
can_you_build: Bir Tawil: land between Egypt and Sudan, so entry is through one of them. Gornja Siga: forest on the Danube, accessible only by crossing Croatian or Serbian border controls, and subject to Croatian policing. Permanent settlement has not been achieved at either.
facts: Bir Tawil: 2,060 km² (Wikipedia).
Boundaries behind it: straight political line of 1899 and irregular administrative line of 1902.
Gornja Siga: about 7 km². The border was drawn by a 1947 commission whose conclusions were never made law (Il Post).
The 2015 Liberland claim attracted hundreds of thousands of citizenship applications, per Vice.

Whether Gornja Siga is true terra nullius is contested. Both States treat it as a border dispute, which is different from renouncing it. We could not retrieve the Croatian or Serbian foreign ministry statements themselves.

name: Antarctica, claimed sectors
who_owns: Seven countries claim sectors, and most others do not recognize those claims. The Antarctic Treaty freezes the argument: claims are neither given up nor strengthened, and nothing done now can create a new one.

rules.says: Peaceful purposes only; no military bases or maneuvers.
No party gives up or loses its claim or position.
Acts or activities while the treaty is in force cannot support or deny a sovereignty claim or 'create any rights of sovereignty', and no new claim may be asserted.
Applies south of 60°S including ice shelves; high-seas rights in the area remain.
Parties must give advance notice of all expeditions organized by their nationals or from their territory.
Any activity relating to mineral resources, other than science, is banned.
Activities need prior environmental impact assessment.
Any Consultative Party can call a review conference after 50 years from entry into force.

hook: Each treaty party must regulate expeditions by its own nationals and those leaving from its territory, including environmental assessment. So your passport country or departure port is the hook. Claimants may treat a sector as theirs, while other parties are free not to recognize that (Art. IV(1)(c)).
can_you_build: Leaving from a treaty party's territory means that party must be told and an impact assessment applies. No land title or sovereignty can come from settling.
facts: Antarctica: 14,200,000 km² (Wikipedia).
Claimants: Argentina, Australia, Chile, France, New Zealand, Norway and the UK, making eight claims (Wikipedia).
Treaty parties: 58, of which 29 are Consultative (decision-making) and 29 Non-Consultative, per the Secretariat.
Treaty in force since 23 June 1961. Protocol in force since 14 January 1998, so the 50-year review point falls in January 2048 (our arithmetic).

name: Antarctica, unclaimed (Marie Byrd Land)
who_owns: No country has claimed it, and the Antarctic Treaty bars any new claim while it is in force. It is the largest unclaimed land on Earth and also the place where a claim is most firmly closed.

rules.says: 'No new claim, or enlargement of an existing claim' may be asserted while the treaty is in force. This binds parties, and acts by anyone cannot create sovereign rights under it.
Expeditions must be notified by the party they come from.
Environmental principles, mineral ban and impact assessment apply here too.

hook: Same as claimed sectors. A non-party individual is still a national of some State, and most routes pass through party territory. The United States and Russia say they keep the right to make claims later, per Wikipedia, which marks one of the two statements as needing a citation.
can_you_build: Wikipedia calls it remote even by Antarctic standards. Getting there means an expedition from a treaty party's territory. Westarctica's claim is catalogued separately.
facts: Area: 1,610,000 km², including the Eights Coast (Wikipedia).
The unclaimed sector lies east of 150°W.

name: Central Arctic Ocean and Svalbard
who_owns: The central Arctic Ocean is high seas surrounded by the EEZs of five coastal States, with UNCLOS applying. Svalbard is Norwegian territory. The 1920 treaty confirms Norway's full sovereignty and gives other parties' nationals equal commercial and access rights.

rules.says: Covers the single high-seas portion surrounded by Canada, Denmark/Greenland, Norway, Russia and the US. Runs for 16 years, with five-year renewals.
A coastal State's shelf can reach past 200 nm under set limits, so seabed under the central Arctic can fall to a coastal State rather than the Area.
Parties recognize Norway's 'full and absolute sovereignty'.
Parties' nationals have equal rights to fishing, hunting, access, trade and mining, subject to local law.
Taxes must be spent on Svalbard itself, and mining rules cannot favor anyone.
No naval base or fortification may be built.

hook: In the ocean: same as the high seas. On Svalbard: Norwegian law and the Governor. Though no visa is needed, Norway can refuse or expel people under its Svalbard regulations, including those without the means to reside there.
can_you_build: On Svalbard a foreigner needs no Norwegian visa or residence permit, and living there gives no sovereign rights. In the central ocean, ice has generally covered the water year-round, though it is shrinking (fisheries agreement preamble).
facts: Svalbard Treaty signed 9 February 1920; 49 parties as of 2026 (Wikipedia).
Fisheries agreement done at Ilulissat 3 October 2018, in force for Canada 25 June 2021.
We did not retrieve the area figure for the Arctic high seas from an official page, so none is given.

name: Airspace over countries
who_owns: The country below. Its sovereignty over the air is complete and exclusive, and territory includes land and territorial waters. No treaty sets how high that goes.

rules.says: Every State has complete and exclusive sovereignty over the airspace above its territory.
Territory means land areas and adjacent territorial waters under a State's sovereignty.
Scheduled international flights need permission from the State flown over or landed in.
Pilotless aircraft need special authorization to overfly a State.
Each State enforces flight rules over its territory and for aircraft bearing its marks, wherever they are.
An aircraft has the nationality of its State of registration, may be registered in one State only, under that State's law, and must display its marks.
Sovereignty covers the air above the territorial sea too.

hook: Art. 1 itself. A country may require any aircraft to land. In February 2023 US jets shot down a Chinese balloon over American airspace. A flying platform without a State of registry has no standing under Art. 17-20.
can_you_build: Only under the local State's permission and registration rules.
facts: ICAO has 193 member States (ICAO page).

Note on the AI statement the user received: 'Earth's atmosphere: underlying country's sovereignty generally applies'. It holds for this zone alone. See airspace-over-high-seas and stratosphere-near-space for what it left out.

name: Airspace over high seas, EEZs and Antarctica
who_owns: Nobody's sovereignty. Overflight is a freedom of all States over the high seas and EEZ, and flight rules come from ICAO standards. Over Antarctica, sovereignty is unsettled because claims are frozen. This is the main gap in the claim that the underlying country's sovereignty 'generally applies'.

rules.says: Freedom of overflight on the high seas.
The same freedom applies over the EEZ.
Air over the Area keeps its status.
'Over the high seas, the rules in force shall be those established under this Convention.'
Piracy and right-of-visit rules extend to aircraft: private aircraft may be seized for piracy, and the visit rules apply to military aircraft.
Claims are frozen, so whether the air above a claimed sector counts as a claimant's airspace is contested by non-recognizers (our reading; the treaties do not address airspace directly).

hook: Registration and nationality: Art. 17-20 tie an aircraft to a State, and that State applies its rules wherever it flies (Art. 12). Every aircraft also has to take off from and land somewhere.
can_you_build: You can fly here with a registered aircraft. A permanently aloft self-governing craft would still need a registry, and without one it has no right to enter any country's airspace.
facts: What the AI claim omitted: (1) over the high seas, about 58.6% of the sea surface, no country has sovereignty; (2) Antarctica's airspace has no settled sovereign; (3) no treaty sets the upper limit of airspace; (4) an EEZ gives no airspace rights, only 12 nm of territorial sea does.

sources.t: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, full text

name: Stratosphere and near space
who_owns: Treated as airspace in practice over a country, with no agreed top. Over high seas, the same freedom applies as lower down. There is no special 'near space' regime in any treaty.

rules.says: No altitude limit is stated.
Outer space cannot be appropriated, though the treaty does not say where outer space begins.
The UN space committee has considered delimitation since 1967 without agreement, and some States oppose defining a line at all.

Australia, Denmark and Kazakhstan use 100 km in space law, and the US has endorsed 100 km for Air Force and Space Force competence, per a 2025 UN submission. New Zealand defines high altitude from flight level 600.

hook: Art. 1, at whatever height the State can reach. The 2023 balloon incident shows States will act at balloon altitude. Launch or balloon flights also start from a State's soil.
can_you_build: Balloons and high-altitude platforms need a launch site, a registry and radio spectrum from a State. This research found no self-governing station at this height.
facts: Kármán line: 100 km, a reference not agreed in law (Library of Congress).
Proposals: 110 km (UN paper A/AC.105/L.168, cited in the submission), 120 km and 160 km for the top of near space.
Most aircraft fly below FL600, about 20 km (Jakarta Post, citing ICAO).

A UN submission states that national airspace has functionally not been legislated beyond 400,000 feet (about 122 km). That language comes from a draft convention by the International Association for the Advancement of Space Safety, and it is not law.

name: Low Earth orbit
who_owns: No country can own it, but every object in it belongs to some State's registry, and that State keeps jurisdiction over it and everyone on it. States are responsible for private activity they license.

rules.says: Space is free for use by all States.
No national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, use, occupation or any other means.
States bear responsibility for private activities, which need authorization and continuing supervision.
Launching States are liable for damage.
The State of registry keeps jurisdiction and control over the object and any personnel on board.
Due regard, and consultation before harmful interference.
The launching State registers each object and reports details to the UN.
Absolute liability for damage on Earth or to aircraft; fault-based liability elsewhere.
Orbits and frequencies are limited natural resources; stations must not cause harmful interference.

hook: You cannot leave Earth without a launch State. That State must authorize you (Art. VI), register you, and keep jurisdiction over your station (Art. VIII). A US citizen launching anywhere outside the US needs an FAA licence (51 USC 50904).
can_you_build: Buy a launch from a licensed operator, which brings a national licensing regime. Radio contact needs an ITU filing through a member State. Resupply comes from Earth (ISS crews still rely on delivered tanks, water and food). Asgardia's satellite claim is catalogued separately.
facts: LEO: under 2,000 km (ESA).
Outer Space Treaty: 118 parties and 23 signatories as at 1 January 2026, up from 116 a year earlier with Latvia and Malaysia. UNOOSA's page lists no later accession.
Registration Convention: 77 parties. Liability Convention: 100 parties, plus 4 organizations by declaration. Rescue Agreement: 100 parties, plus 3 declarations.
ISS: about $3 billion a year to operate (NASA OIG).

name: Geostationary orbit
who_owns: Same as LEO under space law. In practice, orbital slots and frequencies are coordinated through the ITU, whose members are States. Eight equatorial countries tried to claim the slots above them in 1976. Art. II of the space treaty bars appropriation of the orbit by sovereignty claim, which conflicts with that declaration.

rules.says: No appropriation, which covers the orbit.
Members must treat frequencies and orbits, including the geostationary orbit, as limited natural resources with equitable access.
Frequency assignments are recorded in the Master International Frequency Register after notices submitted by national administrations.
Eight equatorial States asserted sovereignty over the part of the orbit above them (Wikipedia).

hook: Spectrum: no filing without a member State's administration. A station without one would have no recorded protection from interference, and operators would have no duty to coordinate with it.
can_you_build: Reaching GEO means a transfer orbit to 35,786 km and then a burn to circularize. Operating there means a State filing and a launch licence.
facts: Altitude: 35,786 km (ESA).
ITU members: 194 States (ITU).
Filings since 7 November 1998 carry cost-recovery fees under Resolution 88 and Council Decision 482.

name: Lagrange points and cislunar space
who_owns: Outer space, so the same regime applies. There is no separate treaty. The Moon Agreement's definition of 'the moon' extends to orbits around it, but only 17 States have joined that agreement.

rules.cite: Outer Space Treaty Art. I, II, VI, VIII
rules.says: Free use, no appropriation, State responsibility, jurisdiction by registry.
References to the Moon include orbits and trajectories around it.

Signatories commit to registration, releasing scientific data, and giving notice of operations inside 'safety zones' to avoid harmful interference. The Accords describe themselves as a political commitment.

hook: Same as LEO. A station here needs a launch State and registry, and it depends on Earth for spectrum and logistics.
can_you_build: The same launch, licence and spectrum steps apply. This research found no published plan for a private settlement here.
facts: Moon distance: about 385,000 km (NASA).
We could not retrieve a NASA page for Lagrange point distances, so none is given.

name: The Moon
who_owns: No country can own it, and treaty parties cannot appropriate it. Sellers of 'deeds' claim private people can own land there, and the International Institute of Space Law has issued a statement warning that buyers may be misled. A second, weaker treaty adds a common-heritage rule for its 17 members, and 78 countries have signed the Artemis Accords, which describe themselves as a political commitment.

rules.says: No national appropriation of the Moon by sovereignty, use, occupation or other means.
Peaceful purposes only on celestial bodies; no military bases, weapons tests or maneuvers.

rules.cite: Outer Space Treaty Art. VI, VIII
rules.says: Private activity needs authorization; a registered object keeps its owner, and the State of registry keeps jurisdiction over it and its staff, on the surface as well.
Avoid harmful contamination and give due regard to others.
Common heritage of mankind. Surface and subsurface cannot become property of any State, organization or person. A future regime is to govern exploitation.
States may build stations, using only the area needed, and must tell the UN.
Signatories say extraction of resources does not in itself count as national appropriation.
Signatories give notice of operations and respect 'safety zones' around them.
US citizens may own and sell space resources they recover, subject to US international obligations.

hook: Art. VI and VIII bind the launching and registering State. The hook is your own State's licensing and your station's registry. Art. II bars national appropriation by any means, and Art. 11(3) of the Moon Agreement bars property in the surface for its parties, so a deed sold by a private person has no treaty behind it (our reading).
can_you_build: Any trip needs a launch licence and ITU spectrum. On the surface you cannot exclude others by right (OST Art. I says free access to all areas), though the Accords' safety zones may in practice limit access.
facts: Artemis Accords: 78 signatories, the latest being Vietnam on 28 October 2026 (NASA).
Moon Agreement: 17 parties and 4 signatories as at 1 January 2026. Saudi Arabia withdrew with effect from 5 January 2024.
Moon Agreement entered into force in July 1984 after Austria became the fifth ratifier.
Moon radius: about 1,740 km; distance about 385,000 km (NASA).
IISL statement: claims of 'deeds to lunar property' raise the chance that individuals will be misled.

name: Asteroids
who_owns: Same as the Moon: no sovereignty, since the treaties cover all celestial bodies. Taking resources is a live question, and US law permits it for its citizens subject to US international obligations.

rules.says: No appropriation of celestial bodies.
Moon rules apply to other solar system bodies for its parties, except Earth.
They do not apply to meteorites that reach Earth naturally.
US citizens may own recovered asteroid resources, subject to US international obligations.
Resource extraction does not in itself count as appropriation.

hook: Same as the Moon. Art. VIII keeps your craft under the registering State's law.
can_you_build: This research found no published settlement project. Fraud has appeared here too: SEC officials in 1999 listed share offerings for exploring a near-Earth asteroid among fraudulent internet schemes.
facts: IISL's statement says deed claims have been extended to other celestial bodies. A deed seller told Discover he owns about 95 planetary bodies.

name: Mars and beyond
who_owns: Same as the Moon under Art. II. Nothing in the Outer Space Treaty ends at the Moon's orbit. A private contract cannot change that. Starlink's beta terms in 2020 said the parties 'recognize Mars as a free planet', and that wording binds only the contract's parties.

rules.cite: Outer Space Treaty Art. II, VI, VIII, IX
rules.says: No appropriation, State supervision, registry jurisdiction, duty to avoid contamination. All are written for 'celestial bodies' generally.
Extends to all solar-system bodies other than Earth, for its parties.
International scientific standard on contamination; latest revision January 2026. It works through national agencies and has no treaty force of its own.

'No Earth-based government has authority or sovereignty over Martian activities' and disputes settle 'through self-governing principles'. This is a private contract term quoted by Universe Today. The current text was not checked.

hook: Launch State, registration and licence on departure. Distance makes enforcement slow, but a State's jurisdiction under Art. VIII continues.
can_you_build: Salotti's 2020 model estimates about 110 people as a minimum for a self-sustaining Mars colony, under its assumptions.
facts: Salotti 2020: minimum of 110 settlers, in Scientific Reports.

name: Digital 'countries' with no territory
who_owns: Each participant stays under the law of wherever they live, and each server sits under the law of where it is. A State needs a defined territory, so a project with none fails one of the four Montevideo tests. It may still function as an association, a company or a club.

rules.says: A defined territory is required.
Statehood does not depend on recognition, but it does depend on Art. 1 criteria.
A country-code domain follows the ISO 3166 list. IANA says it does not decide what is a country.
Passport issuer codes come from the ISO 3166 agency or from separately listed organizations.

hook: Normal domestic law on tax, securities, payments and identity documents. Selling 'citizenships' or tokens brings securities and fraud law, and FATF rules on money transfer.
can_you_build: Anyone can found one, at the cost of a website and a legal wrapper. It can run as a company in a real jurisdiction. Estonia's model runs the other way: a real State holding backup data in a data centre in Luxembourg by agreement with that State.
facts: Asgardia reported more than 290,000 citizens in March 2019 (Wikipedia), with no recognized territory.
Estonia's 'data embassy': a Tier 4 data centre in Luxembourg under a bilateral agreement that takes account of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations.

name: Zones carved out by a host country
who_owns: The host State stays sovereign unless it gives the land away by treaty, and what one legislature grants, a later court or legislature may take back. Vatican City and the Order of Malta show the rare end of the range. Honduras's ZEDEs show the common outcome.

rules.says: Declared unconstitutional the legal basis of ZEDEs, zones exempt from local laws and taxes (Reuters).
Holy See is a non-member observer State, alongside the State of Palestine.
A coastal State may authorize an offshore zone, so this route also works at sea, on its terms.
A 2017 floating city deal, later dropped, per sources listed in Wikipedia and Minnesota JLST.

hook: The host's constitution and the next election. Investors may turn to treaty arbitration: Honduras Próspera Inc.'s ICSID claim was originally $10.775 billion and, per Honduras's Attorney General, has dropped to $1.63 billion.
can_you_build: This is the only route with a working track record for a charter-style city, because it starts with a State's consent. It requires negotiating with a government and accepting its ultimate authority.
facts: ZEDE case: Próspera sits on Roatán, off the Honduran coast.
Claim reduced by about 85%, per the Honduran Attorney General's office as reported by Revista E&N.

The Sovereign Order of Malta describes itself as sovereign and conducts diplomatic relations, and reported relations with 111 countries in 2021. We did not retrieve the Lateran Treaty or the Fort St Angelo agreement.
